content: Vitamin D deficiency was historically a prevalent condition affecting both children and adults residing in industrialized cities. The disease rickets, a manifestation of severe vitamin D deficiency, was first scientifically described in the 17th century by British physicians. In the 20th century, German scientists identified vitamin D and its critical role in maintaining bone health. During this period, the significance of sunlight exposure and dietary measures in preventing rickets was emphasized. The fortification of milk with vitamin D, which began in the 1930s, significantly reduced the prevalence of rickets in the United States, rendering it a rare disease. In 1645, Daniel Whistler, a British physician, provided the first scientific description of vitamin D deficiency in his thesis submitted to the University of Leiden. His work, titled “Inaugural medical disputation on the disease of English children which is popularly termed the rickets,” marked the earliest formal recognition of the condition. In 1650, Francis Glisson, a Cambridge physician, published a detailed Latin treatise, “De Rachitide,” in which he meticulously documented his observations of children suffering from rickets. Later, in 1822, Sniadecki identified a correlation between rickets and insufficient sunlight exposure, noting that children in the inner city of Warsaw exhibited a higher incidence of rickets compared to those in rural areas. In 1918, Mellanby discovered the antirachitic properties of cod liver oil, a breakthrough in understanding the prevention of rickets. By 1922, Elmer McCollum and colleagues distinguished vitamin D from vitamin A and proposed that vitamin D facilitates calcium deposition in bones. In the 1930s, Adolf Otto Reinhold Windaus at the University of Göttingen in Germany elucidated the chemical structure of vitamin D and its precursor, 7-dehydrocholesterol. For his pioneering work on sterols and their relationship to other natural products, Windaus was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1928. Key milestones in the development of treatment strategies for rickets include Sniadecki’s 1822 recognition of the importance of sunlight exposure for both prevention and treatment. In 1890, Theobald Palm advocated for the use of sunbaths to prevent rickets. Mellanby’s 1918 experiments demonstrated that cod liver oil could prevent rickets in puppies. In 1919, Hulschinski observed that exposing children to radiation from a lamp had a therapeutic effect on rickets. In 1921, Hess and Unger exposed seven children with rickets to sunlight in New York City over several months, reporting significant improvement in their condition. By the 1930s, the U.S. government recommended daily sunlight exposure for children as a preventive measure against rickets. During the same decade, the fortification of milk with vitamin D was initiated in the United States and Europe to eradicate rickets. However, an outbreak of hypercalcemia in the 1950s in Great Britain led to the discontinuation of this program in Europe, a decision that remains in effect to this day.
